label: Sikhism
sub: The Guru Granth Sahib and Vaaran Bhai Gurdas
meta: Guru Nanak 1469–1539 · Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan, installed at Amritsar 1604 · Khalsa founded c. 1699 · Guruship vested in the scripture, 1708
history: Sikhism arose in the Punjab with Guru Nanak (1469–1539), who taught devotion to one formless God through remembrance of the divine Name, and was carried forward by a succession of nine further human Gurus. The fifth, Guru Arjan (1563–1606), gathered the hymns of the earlier Gurus, his own, and those of Hindu and Muslim saints; written out by the scribe Bhai Gurdas, whose own Vaaran became the classic early exposition of the faith, this Adi Granth (“First Book”) was installed at Amritsar in 1604. On Baisakhi day, traditionally in 1699, the tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs. He also made the final recension of the scripture, adding the hymns of his father Guru Tegh Bahadur, and before his death in 1708 ended the line of human Gurus, vesting the Guruship in the scripture and the community. The book has since been revered as the Guru Granth Sahib; its standard printed edition runs to 1,430 pages (angs).
impact: There are today about 25 million Sikhs. India’s 2011 census counted nearly 21 million, most of them in Punjab, where they form a majority, and sizeable communities have grown up in Britain, Canada, the United States, Australia and East Africa. The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) at Amritsar is the faith’s holiest shrine, and the adjoining Akal Takht its principal seat of religious authority. Every gurdwara keeps a langar, a free communal kitchen where all may sit and eat together regardless of caste, creed or rank. The scripture is also strikingly plural: beside the Gurus’ hymns it preserves those of fifteen non-Sikh saints of Hindu and Muslim background, among them Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and the Sufi Sheikh Farid — which makes it a natural companion to an ethical text, like the Kural, that many traditions have claimed as their own.
principles: Sikh teaching opens with Ik Onkar, “One Universal Creator”: God is one and formless, without fear or enmity, beyond birth and death, and known through the Guru’s grace. The root human problem is haumai, ego or self-centredness, which feeds the five “thieves” of lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride; it is overcome by living in tune with hukam, the divine order or will. Daily life rests on three pillars: naam japna, remembering and meditating on the divine Name; kirat karni, earning an honest living; and vand chhakna, sharing what one has, expressed above all in seva, selfless service. The Gurus rejected caste distinctions, empty ritual and withdrawal from the world, teaching that liberation is reached as a householder, within family and work. Sikhs accept karma and rebirth, but hold that release from the cycle comes through God’s grace.
